reasons: Witnesses are transmitted text: the Slovo edition text (spi 112: slava gen. sg. + iskati; also spi 25/36 with iskati, čьstь and slava) and the RV Samhita, where RV 1.126.1d, 1.110.5d and 10.102.4c all have śrávas + icchámāna-, a real Vedic formula. Etymology good: iskati and iccháti are the same present formation *h2is-sḱé/ó- (Derksen s.v. *jiskati; EWAia s.v. EṢ'). slava and śrávas share *ḱleu- but are different stems (*ḱlou-eh2 vs *ḱléwos), so that element is root-level only. Collocation congruent: glory as object of seeking, heroic/patron context. Derivative risk is strong: the OCS Gospels (Marianus/Zographensis, John 5:44, 7:18, 8:50) have slava + iskati with the reflexive sebě, translating Greek doxa + zētein. The Slovo is a bookish text, so a Church Slavonic model cannot be excluded, and 'seek glory' is a fairly natural phrase. Defensible, not compelling.
known: Probably discussed: the Slovo's čьstь + slava + iskati passage is a standard item in Slavic/IE poetic-language discussions (Russian Indo-Europeanist literature); the Vedic śrávas + iṣ- formula is well known. Not verified here.

reasons: AM-242-fol 169:9 is the transmitted Skáldskaparmál kenning list. The eye (auga) may be called sól, but also moon, shield, glass, gem or stars, so this is a generic brightness metaphor, not the macrocosm homology of AVŚ 5.9.7 (sūrya- predicated of cakṣus-). Only sól/sūrya is cognate, and auga/cakṣus is renewed. The contexts (metapoetic catalogue vs ritual body-cosmos identification) are not comparable.
known: The eye-sun homology (Puruṣa RV 10.90.13, Ymir) is well discussed (Lincoln, Bruce Lincoln 1975/1986); this kenning is not that figure.

reasons: Anchor (manuscript text DG 8) has dómr as cognate object of dœma, an inner-Germanic figura etymologica (dœma is denominal). Il. 16.387 has θέμιστας with κρίνωσι. θέμις (*dʰh1-mi-) and dómr (*dʰoh1-mo-) share only the root, and the verb is unrelated. 'Judge a judgment' is generic legal diction, and the lead itself calls it insufficiently distinctive.

All loci confirmed as transmitted manuscript or vulgate text. ON: the anchor has setja + kné + reflexive sér (Ásta and Olaf), AM-36 127 has setja + kné + sér (Óláfr and his half-brothers), AM-35 143 has setja + kné (Hákon set on Æthelstan's knee, the fosterage scene). Gk: Il. 9.455 has γούνασιν + οἷσιν + ἐφέσσεσθαι with υἱόν (a curse of never having a son of one's own), Il. 9.488 has γούνεσσι + καθίσσας (Phoenix rearing Achilles), Od. 16.443 has γούνασιν + οἷσιν + ἐφεσσάμενος (Odysseus with the boy Eurymachus). OIr G301012 #8:169 has suidid + glún (Cú Chulainn's fosterage seat). Cognates hold: *ǵonu- (kné, γόνυ; glún < PCelt *glūnos per Matasović, 'beyond doubt'); *sed- in causative setja (*sod-éye-) and the Greek s-aorist ἕσσα 'set'; reflexive *s(w)e- in sér and ἑός. The match is linguistic, not only cultural: verb root + noun + reflexive possessive in the same transitive relation (an adult setting a boy on his own knee), in kin, rearing and fosterage contexts. The lap gesture is natural, which is the generic risk. The anchor scene itself is an interrogation rather than an adoption.
known: Yes: the knee and paternity/adoption complex (Onians 1951; Benveniste; ON knésetja; Hittite Ullikummi, where Kumarbi sets the newborn on his knee and names him, compared with Od. 19.401 by Güterbock and West).

reasons: Text confirmed in two TBC recensions (LL G301035 #1/19:17; LU G301012 #33:5-6; Windisch edition L20465, OCR Bewdacht = Bendacht) as dé + andé in a blessing, with a gloss explaining them as áes cumachta / áes trebaire. RV 6.22.11c is a negated pair, ádeva- ... devá- (neither non-god nor god obstructs). Morphology is parallel (*deiwo- and n̥-privative; dé gen. pl.). But Ved. á-deva- is a possessive 'godless' (of men/demons), while Irish andé is 'non-gods'. The Vedic is a negated nobody-at-all polar expression, the Irish a positive blessing. Privative polar pairs are productive in every IE language. A real shared polar type with cognate material, but not compelling as a shared phrase.
known: The dé + andé crux and its (trifunctional) gloss are much discussed in Irish scholarship (Dumézil-school; Mac Cana); polar expressions in general by Watkins. Not verified here.

reasons: Anchor (DG 8 dream prophecy) has hrafn + hræ + vargr with slíta. MBh 3.48.71-73 is the close thematic parallel (beasts and vultures eat the enemies' māṃsa and drink their rudhira) but has no cognate material. MBh 2.71.58 (kravyād-, gṛdhra-, gomāyu-, vāyasa-) is an omen list, not a threat. hræ ~ kravis- is accepted by Kroonen (*krou(h2)-io-, irregular metathesis), but hræ 'corpse' and kravyād- 'flesh-eater' are not in the same relation. This is the general beasts-of-battle motif, not carried by cognate wording.
known: Beasts-of-battle / 'dogs and birds' theme widely discussed (Magoun; Homeric scholarship; West).

reasons: Same anchor and motif as L006. Il. 22.335/22.354 (κύνες + οἰωνοί, with ἑλκήσουσι / δάσονται) are a genuine thematic match: a threat to a falling warrior that canines and carrion birds will tear him. AM-242 106:17 (Huginn/Muninn, hræ) is mythological. No element is cognate (hrafn/οἰωνός, vargr/κύων), so this is a renewed motif, not inherited wording.
known: Yes: the corpse-exposure / beasts-of-battle theme is a known comparison.

reasons: Anchor (DG 8) has hjarta as subject with berja (the heart beaten out of you = you are cowed). Il. 10.94-95 has κραδίη + ἐκθρῴσκει (the heart leaps from the chest in anxiety). Only *ḱerd- is cognate, the predicates differ in meaning and agency, and fear-heart idioms are universal.

AM-56-4to (manuscript text, law of inheritance) has koma + ljós (a child born alive into the light and baptized). Lucretius 1.170 and 5.224 have Ennian luminis + orae. ljós and lūmen share only *leuk- (different derivatives). 'Come into the light' for birth is generic, and in Christian legal prose it is open to Latin influence (lux).
known: 'See the light = live' imagery is discussed by West (IEPM); the Ennian/Lucretian formula is well known.

reasons: Anchor (DG 8) has namn + bera (bear the title of king). Herodotus 1.32.9 has οὔνομα + φέρεσθαι (carry off the title of happy man), and Euripides Hel. 66 has ὄνομα + δυσκλεές + φέρω. Both elements are exact cognates (*h1nómn̥, *bʰer-; Kroonen s.vv. *namon-, *beran-) in the same verb-object relation, with name = title/status, so the figure is real. But 'bear a name' is easily re-formed, and the Herodotean middle means 'win' rather than 'hold'. ON usage clusters in learned and legal prose, where Latin nomen + ferre/gerere could be the model.
known: The *h1nómn̥ + *dʰeh1- 'put a name' collocation is well known; for *bʰer- + name I know of no specific discussion.

reasons: Same figure as L004. On its own evidence it is weaker. Od. 19.401 has γούνασι + θῆκε (Eurykleia puts the newborn on Autolykos' knees before he names him), so the knee noun is cognate but the verb is renewed. The ON–OIr pair has *sed- (setja, suidid) and *ǵonu- (kné, glún), but in different relations: ON causative 'set on (á) the knee' vs Irish intransitive 'sit under (fo) the knee'. Defensible, not compelling on these witnesses alone.
known: Yes (see L004): Od. 19.401 vs Hittite Ullikummi knee-naming is a known comparison.

reasons: Anchor (Njáls saga, AM-162 B kappa, manuscript text) has unna + auga with sem (love her as the eyes in his head). Catullus 3.5 and 14.1 have plus + oculis + amare. Only auga/oculus is cognate. The verbs are renewed and the comparison type differs (equative vs comparative). 'Dear as one's eyes' is a widespread commonplace (Hellenistic Greek, biblical apple of the eye).
known: The Catullan oculus-comparison commonplace and its Greek parallels are standard commentary material (e.g. Fordyce ad 3.5).

reasons: Anchor (DG 8, a Christian vision) has hvítr + sem + snjór of a face. Catullus 80.2 has candidior + nix. Only the snow noun is cognate, and the adjectives differ. 'White as snow' is universal and biblical (Mt 28:3, Dan 7:9, Rev 1:14), the likely hagiographic model.

Anchor (DG 8 healing miracle) has léttr + fótr with mjúkr. The Homeric formula (Il. 5.122, 13.61, 23.772) has ἐλαφρά + πόδας with γυῖα + ἔθηκεν, twice after a granted prayer. Two cognate stems: léttr ~ ἐλαφρός (*h1legʷʰ-, different suffixes; Kroonen s.v. *linhta-) and fótr ~ πούς. But in Homer πόδας is an accusative of respect to γυῖα, while the ON foot is the subject. A light foot after healing is natural and generic, and the witness is a hagiographic miracle with Latin models.

Vǫluspá (GKS 2365, manuscript text) has ósáinn + akr + vaxa. Od. 9.109/9.123 have ἄσπαρτος + ἀνήροτος, AVŚ 5.29.13 has akṛṣṭapacya-, Hesiod WD 118 has αὐτομάτη. No cognate in any slot. A golden-age or renewed-world motif, possibly Christian-apocalyptic in Vǫluspá. The lead itself makes no claim.
known: The golden-age 'unsown' motif is known (Vǫluspá's ósáinn + akr is often compared with Hesiod and Christian paradise imagery).

reasons: Wrong etymology. ON ormr < PGmc *wurmi- < *wr̥mi- (= Lat. vermis; Kroonen s.v. *wurmi-), while Skt. kṛ́mi- < *kʷr̥mi- (OIr. cruim, Lith. kirmis). EWAia s.v. kṛ́mi- treats *wr̥mi- as a separate taboo rhyme formation (after Watkins), not a cognate. The verbs are unrelated too (vega vs han-). Anchor (DG 8) is an ekphrasis of Sigurðr killing the serpent, and AVŚ 2.32.1/7 is a worm charm (krimi- + han-), so the contexts are not comparable.
known: Dragon-slaying formula (*gʷʰen- + *h1ógʷʰi-) is Watkins' How to Kill a Dragon; the AV worm charms are discussed there. This lead does not instantiate that formula.

reasons: Same figure as L012, and AM-132 48v:10 is another manuscript of the same Njáls passage, not an independent ON witness. Catullus 3.5, 14.1, 82.2/82.4 and 104.2 (carus + oculis) are confirmed. Only the eye noun is cognate. A generic commonplace, and the Latin is possibly Greek-influenced.

Anchor (AM-35, manuscript text) has blómi + aldr (genitive), of King Haraldr. Lucretius 3.770 and 5.847 have aetas (gen.) + flos, and Il. 13.484 has ἥβη + ἄνθος. blómi ~ flōs share *bʰleh3- (different stems), and aldr/aetas are not cognate but equivalent, in the same flower-of-age genitive construction. But the metaphor is generic, and medieval Latin flos aetatis is a likely model for the ON, so derivation is a serious alternative.
known: 'Flower of youth' (ἥβη + ἄνθος) is discussed in Homeric and IE poetics (West).

reasons: Anchor (LL TBC) has tregtad + cride + clíab (heart pierced in his chest). Il. 13.442 has δόρυ + κραδίη + ἐπεπήγει, and Od. 1.341 has στῆθος + κῆρ. Only the heart noun is cognate, and clíab and στῆθος are unrelated. A spear in the heart is literal anatomy in any battle narrative.

Revue Celtique 6 edition text confirmed (OCR Id for lá): Lóegaire's sureties are paired grían/éscae, uisce/áer, lá/adaig, muir/tír. Lucretius 3.837 has terra + mare (terra marique), and 2.1085 and 5.115 list world-parts. Both members are cognate: muir ~ mare (*mori-, Matasović) and tír ~ terra (*ters-, de Vaan). But land-and-sea is a near-universal merism, and the contexts differ: elemental guarantee in an oath vs cosmological catalogue or the stock Latin adverbial. At most an Italo-Celtic lexical pair; the figure is generic.
known: Lóegaire's elemental oath is well known (cf. elements as guarantors, Il. 3.276-280; discussed by Mac Cana, Watkins). Not verified here.

reasons: Same figure as L004, but graded on its own evidence. The anchor (DG 8 0027:2) has taka + kné + sér: the verb is taka 'take', not setja, so the anchor carries only the knee noun and the reflexive. The *sed- verb comes from ON partners (same language) and Il. 9.455. Od. 19.401 renews it (θῆκε). The kin and naming/fosterage function is congruent, but on this lead's own material there is one cross-branch lexical cognate plus the reflexive. Weak. The figure's strength is assessed under L004.

Same figure as L010. RV 1.103.4b and 5.30.5b have nā́man- + bíbhrat with kīrtényam / śrútyam (bearing a name to be praised / heard), confirmed, and AM-302 (law) has nafn + bera with bóndi. Exact cognates nafn/nā́man- and bera/bhr̥- in a verb-object relation, with overlapping semantics. But the Vedic is 'bearing a famous name' while the ON is 'holding the status of king/farmer', in learned/legal prose open to Latin nomen + ferre/gerere. Generic collocation.

Same figure, anchor and Homeric loci as L014 (Il. 5.122, 13.61, 23.772). Cognate pairs léttr/ἐλαφρός and fótr/πούς, divine or saintly restoration after prayer. But the syntax differs (accusative of respect vs subject), 'light feet' is generic, and the ON is a hagiographic miracle.

Same figure as L013. Anchor (DG 8) has hvítr + sem + snjór of a sail, and Catullus 80.2 has candidior + nix of lips. Only snow is cognate and the referents differ. A universal colour simile, also biblical.

AM-36 386:01 (Óttarr svarti, manuscript text) has úlfr (gen.) + beita (wolf's food, a battle-praise kenning). RV 10.95.14d has vŕ̥ka- + ad- (wolves would eat him, Purūravas' death wish). Only the wolf noun (*wl̥kʷo-) is cognate, and beita (*bʰeid-) and ad- (*h1ed-) are not. Feeding the wolf is the generic beasts-of-battle commonplace, and the contexts are not comparable.
